items.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000
items.q: Incidentally I saw them once, I think it was at Monterey... Paul came back and he was stoned... he stood up and he played his brains out.

ctx.x: Yeah we hired a new agency, an ad agency, and we got to talking about jazz, and I said I know a lot of jazz guys and so on and so forth. The guy says well I’ll put you to the test. So he brought in the record the “Four Brothers.” And they set it up in the room next door a couple of weeks later. And he brought me in and said, “Now what is this?” I says, “That’s the ‘Four Brothers,’” and then I named the four sax players. He died. He died. Well that’s a sterling tune. That’s really good. Ellington — I’d take a…

was stoned. Either drunk or out on dope or something, and he came back and he sat there at the stand, just out of it. Everybody’s playing the set, and they started the “Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue” and they got to the sax solo, all of a sudden he came to, he stood up and he played his brains out. Amazing.
